Latest from the NBER

Helena Foulkes Elected Governor of Rhode Island

news article

Helena Foulkes, an at-large member of the NBER board of directors since April 2020, was elected Governor of Rhode Island on November 3, 2026. She received more than 57 percent of the votes, nearly 30 percent more than any other candidate. In light of her new responsibilities, she has resigned from the NBER board.

Foulkes is the former CEO of the Hudson's Bay Company, a retail conglomerate. She spent nearly 25 years as an executive at CVS Health, where her roles included President of CVS Pharmacy and Executive Vice President of CVS Health. She holds an AB in Economics from Harvard College and an MBA from the Harvard Business School. She has served as a director of The Home Depot and on the Board of Overseers of Harvard University.

A research summary from the monthly NBER Digest

Immigration and Productivity Growth in the OECD

article

Birth rates across Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries have fallen in recent decades and native working-age populations have begun to shrink. At the same time, immigration—particularly from lower- and middle-income countries outside the OECD—has risen sharply. It has become the main source of labor force growth in much of Europe. In Immigration and Macroeconomic Outcomes in OECD Countries (NBER Working Paper 35523), Gaetano Basso, Mitali R. Mathur, and Giovanni Peri examine how immigration…

From the NBER Bulletin on Health

Why Has US Healthcare Expenditure Growth Slowed?

article

Between 2010 and 2024, medical spending in the US grew from 17.2 percent of GDP to 18.0 percent. This growth was substantially below both historical precedent and actuarial projections by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS). By 2024, annual healthcare expenditures were nearly $1 trillion (15 percent) below the 2010 projections. 

In Has the United States Bent the Health Care Cost Curve? (NBER Working Paper 35231), David M. Cutler and Lev R. Klarnet examine potential explanations for this sustained period of slower growth. They compare actual expenditures to the 2010 CMS actuarial forecast, adjusting for differences between anticipated and realized…

From the NBER Bulletin on Entrepreneurship

Entrepreneurship Training Can Help Founders Learn When to Quit

article

Entrepreneurship training is generally intended to improve founders’ chances of success. It may also create value by helping entrepreneurs recognize when a venture no longer warrants further investment of time and resources. If so, effective training could cause some startups to shut down sooner even as it improves outcomes for others. 

In Learning to Quit? A Multi-Year, Multi-Site Field Experiment with Innovation-Driven Entrepreneurs (NBER Working Paper 34755), Esther Bailey, Daniel Fehder, Eric Floyd, Yael Hochberg, and Daniel J. Lee study this possibility through a randomized experiment ...

From the NBER Reporter: Research, program, and conference summaries

Social Security Reform in an Era of Fiscal Deficits 18th Annual Feldstein Lecture, July 29, 2026

article

I am deeply honored to be here with you today to deliver the 2026 Martin Feldstein lecture. I first met Marty more than 30 years ago in the Fall of 1995 as a graduate student in his Public Economics course. I learned so much from him during that course about Social Security and many other topics including individual and corporate income taxation, unemployment insurance, and public goods. I also was fortunate during the next three years of my graduate studies to serve as a Teaching Fellow in both his Principles of Economics and American Economic Policy courses and to have him as one of my advisors on my PhD research. He was a phenomenal teacher and advisor who cared deeply about all of his students. This dedication extended to the entire academic economics profession as evidenced by his inspiring leadership for many years of the NBER…

From the NBER Bulletin on the Economics of Alzheimer's Disease

Probable Dementia and Health Insurance Choices

article

Nearly one in ten older Americans lives with dementia, a condition that gradually erodes memory and the cognitive skills needed for complex decision-making. Even though Medicare coverage is nearly universal among this age group, traditional Medicare alone leaves significant gaps as it does not cover dental, vision, or hearing care, and it carries substantial cost-sharing. To fill these gaps, beneficiaries must actively choose among several insurance options—enrolling in Medicare Advantage, adding private supplemental insurance to traditional Medicare, or, for those with sufficiently low income and assets, applying for Medicaid. Beneficiaries may make changes during open enrollment each year and must re-enroll in private supplemental coverage or Medicare Advantage if their plan is no longer offered or they fail to pay premiums…

Featured Working Papers

Cross-Border Learning in Semiconductors
November 13, 2026

Pinelopi Koujianou Goldberg, Réka Juhász, Giulia Lo Forte, and Jeff Thurk find that semiconductor know-how crosses borders mainly through supply-chain partnerships, engineers moving within multinationals, and foreign direct investment.

Concentration of Award-Winning Economists
November 12, 2026

Among nearly 6,000 prizewinning researchers in 18 fields, economics is the only one in which award winners have become more concentrated at a few institutions since 1960, according to Richard B. Freeman, Danxia Xie, Hanzhe Zhang, and Hanzhang Zhou. 

The Cost of the AI Buildout
November 11, 2026

Building 188 gigawatts of US AI data capacity by 2032, the amount that current corporate projections suggest, will require nearly $9 trillion in investment, or 3.2 percent of GDP per year from 2025 to 2032, according to Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh.

Oil Shocks and the US as a Net Exporter
November 10, 2026

The shale revolution turned the US from a petroleum importer into a net exporter and as a result oil supply shocks went from contracting the US economy to expanding it, according to Diego R. Känzig, James H. Stock, and Luca Zanotti.

AI Writing in PhD Dissertations
November 9, 2026

AI-generated writing was absent from US STEM dissertations before 2023 but appears in 29 percent of those filed in 2026. Graduates whose dissertations contain AI writing are less likely to enter academic research careers than other graduates without such writing, according to Daniel P. Gross, Dror Shvadron, and Hansen Zhang.
